query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At high temperatures (500–700°C), a controlled thermal pre-oxidation treatment of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings specifically promotes the formation of a continuous, nanocrystalline Cr/Cu-rich oxide tribolayer that acts as a self-lubricating barrier, thereby reducing friction and wear under high-load conditions compared to as-deposited coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film protective coating in its as-deposited state.
generation.intervention: Apply a thermal pre-oxidation treatment (e.g., heat to ~500°C for a defined duration in a controlled atmosphere) to induce oxide layer formation prior to exposure to wear conditions.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear testing in the range of 500°C to 700°C under elevated contact loads representative of demanding protective applications (e.g., in drilling fluid environments).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a nanocrystalline, adherent oxide layer enriched in Cr and Cu that covers the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: The pre-oxidation treatment triggers selective oxidation of Cr and Cu, generating an oxide film that reduces direct metal–metal contact and minimizes the effects of adhesive and abrasive wear. This oxide layer acts as a self-lubricating barrier by reducing friction and inhibiting plastic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, the treated coatings will display significantly lower wear rates and friction coefficients during high-temperature wear tests. Surface analyses (using TEM and XPS) should reveal a well-adhered, continuous, nanoscale Cr/Cu-rich oxide layer that correlates with the enhanced wear performance.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without any thermal pre-oxidation treatment, subjected to identical high-temperature, high-load wear conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold under high-temperature (500–700°C) and high-load scenarios. At temperatures exceeding this range or if the oxidation becomes excessive, the oxide layer might become brittle or spall off, compromising wear resistance.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal pre-oxidation temperature, duration, and atmospheric conditions for forming the ideal oxide layer are not yet fully established and may vary with deposition method and substrate; further optimization is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on similar substrates. Apply a thermal pre-oxidation treatment (e.g., heating at ~500°C for an optimized time) to one group while leaving the other group as-deposited. Subject both groups to uniform high-temperature (500–700°C) and high-load wear tests that simulate realistic conditions (e.g., in a corrosive or particle-containing environment).
measurements: Quantitative wear rate evaluation (volume loss measurements)
Friction coefficient tracking during wear tests using a tribometer
Surface characterization post-test via TEM and XPS to assess the presence, continuity, and composition (Cr/Cu enrichment) of the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if (1) the pre-oxidation treatment does not result in the formation of a continuous, nanocrystalline Cr/Cu-rich oxide layer, or (2) the wear rates and friction coefficients of the treated coatings are not significantly lower than those of the as-deposited coatings under identical conditions.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Phase Structure and Morphology of CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy Coating
cited_evidence.text: Figure 7 shows the microhardness distribution curves of CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings prepared by CS and HVOF, and the coatings heat-treated at different temperatures. Both coatings reach the highest hardness at 500 °C, 487.6 HV0.1 for CS coating and 352.4 HV0.1 for HVOF coating. At 700 °C and 900 °C, the hardness of both coatings is lower than that at room temperature. This is because the heat treatment at 500 °C makes the coating form a heterogeneous structure composed of nanotwins in the recrystallized grains, and high-density dislocations appear in the deformation region. When the annealing temperature exceeds 500 °C, the coating exhibits a completely recrystallized structure, the yield stress decreases and the hardness decreases.

The wear rates of the two coatings at room temperature are very close. The wear rate for the CS and HVOF coatings reaches its the lowest point after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C. The wear rate of the CS-500 °C coating is 0.2152 mm3 m−1 N−1, which is about 4/5 (0.2651 mm3 m−1 N−1) of that of the HVOF-500 °C coating. The CS coating with 500 °C vacuum heat treatment has the best wear resistance due to having the highest microhardness. The wear rates and wear amounts of the two coatings heat-treated at 700 °C and 900 °C decreases due to the decrease in microhardness. The wear mechanisms of the CS and HVOF coatings before and after vacuum heat treatment are adhesive wear, abrasive wear, fatigue wear and oxidation wear.

frame.understanding: Hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu coatings is governed by the thermally activated formation of a nanoscale, adherent oxide or tribolayer—primarily involving elements such as Cr and Cu—that acts as a self-lubricating barrier. Intervention: Introduce a thermal pre-oxidation treatment relative to a baseline as-deposited coating to deliberately promote controlled formation of this oxide film. Expected observations if the hypothesis is true include: (1) under high-temperature (500°C–700°C) and high-load wear conditions, the pre-treated coating should exhibit significantly reduced wear rates compared to the untreated baseline; (2) analytical techniques (e.g., TEM, XPS) would reveal a continuous, nano-crystalline, multi-element oxide layer that directly correlates with reduced friction and wear; (3) microstructural analysis should show that the oxide acts to inhibit plastic deformation and abrasion. This hypothesis builds on prior evidence suggesting that microstructural features (grain size and phase formation) impact wear at room temperature and leverages known oxidation behaviors in similar alloys. A falsifying result would be if the pre-oxidation treatment fails to produce a stable, adherent oxide layer, or if, despite its formation, there is no measurable improvement—or even degradation—in wear performance compared to the untreated coating under the specified test conditions.

decision.trend: Earlier studies of high-entropy alloy coatings have mainly tuned room‐temperature properties via variations in composition, grain size, and deposition/substrate combinations. In several works, post‐processing such as vacuum heat treatments (e.g., PMC9820961) was shown to alter microstructural phases and mechanical properties, with evidence that thermally induced phase or surface layer changes (for example, oxide formation) can lower wear and friction. However, these treatments were mostly used to enhance hardness and adhesion rather than explicitly correlating a deliberately engineered, thermally activated oxide/tribolayer with improved high‐temperature wear resistance.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved whether, under high-temperature and high-load conditions, a purposely pre-formed nanoscale, adherent oxide (or tribolayer) in FeNiCrCoCu coatings can systematically serve as a self-lubricating barrier that mitigates wear. In other words, while many studies linked microstructure (grain size, phase content) to room-temperature wear, the exact mechanistic role of thermally activated oxide layer formation on the overall wear resistance at elevated temperatures has not been directly tested.
decision.lever: Implement a thermal pre-oxidation treatment on FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings (adjusting temperature and exposure time to promote formation of a continuous, nanoscale Cr/Cu-rich oxide layer) versus a baseline as-deposited sample.
decision.why: This step directly follows the identified gap and trend: prior evidence indicates that controlled heat treatments can modify surface layers and improve wear properties (as in PMC9820961), and the testable hypothesis is that, at high temperatures (500°C–700°C) under high load, the deliberately engineered oxide tribolayer will reduce friction and wear. Improved adhesion and lower wear rates along with surface characterization (via TEM/XPS) showing an intact, self-lubricating oxide film would support this mechanism; failure to form such a layer or lack of improvement would falsify the hypothesis.
